title: Event Triggered Execution: Application Shimming
summary: The Application Compatibility Infrastructure sits between a program's import table and the operating system, so that old software keeps working on a new build. Shims are grouped into databases with the sdb extension, held in the AppPatch folder, and the installed and custom sets are registered under the compatibility flags area of the registry; administrators install custom databases with the sdbinst utility. When a matching program starts, the compatibility engine consults the database and hooks the calls named in it. Certain shims are far more powerful than a compatibility fix: they can start another executable, load a library into the process, or switch off memory and exception protections such as Data Execution Prevention and Structured Exception Handling, which also makes them useful for bypassing User Account Control. The artefacts are sdbinst execution, new or changed database files, the matching registry keys and unusual module loads inside the shimmed process. Legitimate shims are few, documented and change-controlled, so volume and timing are the best discriminators.

beginner.definition: This technique uses a Windows compatibility feature called a shim. A shim is a small rule that changes how a program behaves, so older software still works on a newer Windows. Shims are stored in database files, and an administrator installs them with a tool named sdbinst. An attacker installs their own database. Then Windows applies the attacker's rule to a chosen program.
beginner.whyItMatters: Some shims are not simple fixes. They can start another program, load a library, or switch off memory protections for a process. Those same abilities help an attacker bypass User Account Control or hide code inside another program. Because shims run in user mode, they look less alarming than a kernel driver. If you never review installed databases, a powerful rule can sit on the machine for a long time.
howItWorks: Windows keeps a compatibility framework that sits between a program and the operating system.
A shim is a rule that changes how a chosen program behaves, so old software still runs.
Shims are grouped into database files with the sdb ending in the application patch folder.
An administrator installs a database with sdbinst, and the registry records the new entry.
When a matching program starts, the framework loads its shims and redirects the chosen calls.
Some shims can start another program, load a library, or disable memory protections for that process.
beginner.example: Think of a building with a helpful door steward. The steward keeps a notebook listing old shops that cannot use the new automatic doors, so he opens a side door for them. His notebook is the only record of who gets that help. If someone edits the notebook, the steward will happily open a locked staff door for the wrong shop. Application shims are that notebook: useful for legacy programs, and dangerous once the wrong person can write in it.
takeaways: Shims are compatibility rules stored in database files, and administrators install them with sdbinst.
Some shims can start programs, load libraries or weaken memory protections.
Keep a list of approved shim databases and investigate every new one.

objectives: Explain what a shim is and why the compatibility framework exists.
Describe how a shim database is installed and recorded in the registry.
Identify the powerful shims that change privileges or memory protections.
Detect the installation of an unexpected shim database.
Separate approved legacy compatibility rules from attacker-installed ones.
Explain why a user-mode shim can still be dangerous.
